note: Every read of the spine store MERGES and every write MERGES FIRST. That is deliberate -- it is what lets N save-then-exit processes compose instead of clobbering -- and it has a consequence nobody wrote down: the store is MONOTONE. It can express 'this key has a value' and cannot express 'this key is gone'. Observed, not reasoned: purge_fixtures() removed 56 entries across five tables and the very next save_spine_state() restored all 14 fixture keys. So a purge reported success and changed nothing durable. Deletion was not buggy, it was UNREPRESENTABLE. Generalised: any merge-on-both-sides store has no vocabulary for absence, and every removal operation on it will look like it worked.

Standard CRDT answer: record the removal as a fact. A tombstone set, persisted in the payload and shipped in the gossip envelope, so a merge that sees an absent key can ask whether it was never written or deliberately removed. The first pass enforced it on every MERGE path -- both disk loads, the gossip merge, audit_state -- and I wrote that up as done. Re-reading the enforcement sites is what caught the gap: merge-only enforcement holds against the filesystem and against a peer, and NOT against the live process. A record_outcome for a purged key re-created it in the very tables the purge had cleared, and the next save wrote it back out. Step: for any invariant, enumerate the paths that can VIOLATE it (write paths), not the paths that can PROPAGATE it (merge paths). I had audited the second and called it the first.

Where to put the write-path guard. The tempting move is to guard record_outcome, the hot path where the bug was observed. But dream_reinforce reaches the Q kernel WITHOUT passing through record_outcome -- the offline-learning channel would have stayed open, and the fixture would have returned via dreams. Chose choke points instead: ONE guard per table, at the single place every writer must funnel through (_q_observe_unlocked for Q -- the target, delta, and simulated forms all reduce to it; record_outcome for the homeostat, since that is where the record is created). Three guards that can drift apart became two that cannot. Generalised: a guard belongs at the narrowest point every violator must cross, not at the site where the first violation was seen.

The guard returns early. A bare return would make 'a fixture is still being exercised by live code' indistinguishable from 'nothing happened' -- the exact silent-failure class the mesh audit spent a session removing, now reintroduced by my own fix. So refusals are counted per key and exposed via purged_blocked_writes(), and the reset path clears the counter so tests cannot leak. Reused the silence.py reasoning verbatim: a swallowed no-op is indistinguishable from a healthy key. Note the counter is a FINDING ABOUT THE CALLER, not a fault in the tombstone -- a nonzero count means a fixture name is still being exercised, which is information an operator wants and cannot currently get any other way.

The new test proves absence -- record_outcome on a purged key leaves it absent. Absence assertions are exactly the shape that passed on the BROKEN code in the G6 synapse case, whenever no writer happened to run. So the suite carries a third test that DISABLES the predicate (_purged_blocked -> always False, which is precisely the pre-fix behaviour) and asserts the key DOES return. That converts 'the key stayed away' into 'the guard is why the key stayed away'. Verified running: 8 passed, including the load-bearing one. Generalised rule: for any guard, ship the test that removes the guard and shows the defect returning; otherwise a passing suite is evidence about the test, not about the code.

tests/test_spine_mesh.py HANGS. Its first appearance was as a 600s timeout on a multi-suite run, which is exactly the situation where the newest change gets blamed. Attribution procedure that worked: simulate the pre-fix behaviour in-process (patch _purged_blocked to always False, so the new guard is inert) and re-run. It hung identically with the guard disabled, so the hang is not caused by the guard predicate. I still cannot say what does cause it -- only what does not -- and reporting the weaker true claim is the correct move. Generalised: before fixing a failure, attribute it; disabling your own change in-process is a cheaper discriminator than a revert under a concurrent writer.

A second assistant is editing the same working tree. Two decisions followed from that and neither is technical. First, the highest-value targets (canonical docs, the catalog, test files) are exactly the shared files a second writer would touch, so the edit style has to change even though the goal does not: appends and new files instead of rewrites, plus small uniquely-anchored in-place fixes, because a str_replace whose anchor has been edited by the other writer FAILS SAFELY rather than clobbering. Second, the shell timeouts are contention, not breakage -- evidenced by commands succeeding in bursts after quiet periods. Step: when a shared resource behaves intermittently, check for a second writer before debugging the resource.

Staleness was measurable without any external source of truth, because the artifacts contradict THEMSELVES. SKILLS_CATALOG.md claims 1,224 total in its Inventory Summary while its own 'Skill Quick Reference' table holds 1,259 rows. AZAZAEL_INSIGHTS.md section 1 says 226 worms / 35 categories while section 7 says 104 / 18. MANDATES.md says '30 mandates' in its header and '37 total mandates codified' in its own footer. Measured against disk: .agents/skills holds 1,261 entries (968 pkg + 74 pkg314t + 46 bin + 139 core azazael-* + 34 other), canonical skills/ holds 1,226. Rule: a document that disagrees with itself is stale regardless of what the world says, and the internal cross-check is available before any count is taken -- so 'is this doc stale' is answerable in seconds, and the answer is usually an arithmetic contradiction rather than a missing paragraph.

The append-only constraint turned out to improve the documentation rather than constrain it. The instinct was to rewrite AZAZAEL_INSIGHTS.md section 7's stale metrics in place. Appending instead forces the new section to say WHAT it supersedes and WHY, which preserves the trail of a number that was once believed -- and that trail is the only evidence that the metrics drift at all. A corrected figure with no record of its predecessor is indistinguishable from a figure that was always right. Generalised: corrections should carry their own provenance, because a document that silently becomes accurate teaches nobody how it became inaccurate.
